egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese, meat, tomatoes and dark‑green vegetables, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of eggs cooked without added fat, combined with cheese, lean meat, tomatoes and dark‑green vegetables (such as spinach or broccoli). Eggs provide high‑quality protein, while the vegetables and tomatoes add vitamins, minerals and dietary fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the most nutrient‑dense foods, containing all essential amino acids.
A modest amount of cheese boosts calcium and vitamin D content.
Lean meat (e.g., turkey or chicken breast) adds extra protein without excess fat.
Dark‑green vegetables are rich in lutein and zeaxanthin, beneficial for eye health.
The dish can be prepared on a dry pan, using the natural moisture of the eggs.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Eggs and meat supply a complete set of amino acids that support tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs provide vitamin B12, while meat adds niacin and riboflavin, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Bone support
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium and vitamin D, which help maintain strong bones.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Tomatoes and dark‑green vegetables contain lycopene, lutein and vitamin C, which combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Low added‑fat content
items.content: Cooking without oil reduces overall calories and saturated fat intake.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with hyperlipidemia should monitor yolk consumption.

items.title: Sodium in cheese
items.content: Cheeses can be salty; choose low‑sodium, reduced‑fat varieties when possible.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Use fresh, lean meat to avoid the risk of food‑borne infections.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Beat the eggs, then stir in chopped tomatoes, cheese, pre‑cooked meat pieces and finely sliced green vegetables. Pour the mixture onto a pre‑heated dry skillet, cook over medium heat, gently stirring until the eggs set. Serve immediately while hot.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The dish is best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours and reheat in a skillet or microwave before serving.

shrimp-in-garlic-sauce-puerto-rican-styl.title: Shrimp in Garlic Sauce, Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp in garlic sauce, Puerto Rican style is a dish of large peeled shrimp sautéed in a fragrant sauce made from garlic, olive oil, lime, cilantro and spices typical of Puerto Rican cuisine. The result is a bright, slightly spicy flavor with citrus and herb notes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Puerto Rican cuisine blends Spanish, African and Indigenous influences, reflected in the use of garlic, lime and cilantro.
The garlic sauce is often based on olive oil and vinegar, making it lighter than creamy sauces.
Shrimp are one of the most popular seafoods in the Caribbean due to their fast growth and availability.
Traditionally the dish is served with rice, beans or fried plantains.
In Puerto Rico a “mojo” sauce—garlic and olive oil based—is commonly used as a base for this dish.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Shrimp provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other seafood, shrimp contain very little saturated fat.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium supports immune function and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Shrimp are rich in vitamin B12 and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Small amounts of EPA and DHA contribute to heart and brain health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Foodborne toxins
items.content: Improperly stored shrimp can harbor bacteria and toxins that cause food poisoning.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: If the sauce includes soy sauce or added salt, the dish can become high in sodium.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main course or appetizer. Shrimp in garlic sauce pairs well with rice, quinoa, fried plantains or a fresh salad. Squeeze additional lime juice before serving to brighten the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag and use within a month. Reheat thoroughly until the shrimp are hot throughout.

content.title: About
content.content: Watercress (Nasturtium officinale) is a leafy vegetable that grows in flowing water. It has bright green leaves, a mildly peppery taste, and a crunchy texture. Watercress is usually eaten raw in salads, smoothies, and as a garnish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Watercress is considered one of the most nutrient‑dense leafy greens.
It naturally occurs in streams and rivers across Europe, Asia, and North America.
Ancient Romans used it as a medicinal herb for colds.
It is exceptionally high in vitamin C – about 70 mg per 100 g, more than oranges.
The leaves can be used as a natural food coloring.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate supports cell division and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: High in antioxidants
items.content: Watercress provides carotenoids and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Low‑calorie fiber source
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Water‑borne contamination
items.content: Because it grows in streams, watercress can be contaminated with bacteria or parasites; thorough washing is recommended.

items.title: Interaction with blood thinners
items.content: High vitamin K content may reduce the effectiveness of anticoagulant medications.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergy symptoms such as rash or swelling.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add watercress to fresh salads, sandwiches, smoothies, soups, or use it as a garnish for fish and meat dishes. Before eating, rinse the leaves well under running water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store watercress in the refrigerator in an airtight container or a bag with a small amount of moisture. It stays fresh for 3–5 days. Discard if leaves turn yellow or develop an off‑odor.
